title: AC Circuits: Pure Capacitor, Power in L/C, LR Circuit, RC Circuit, Numericals

claims.text: AC circuit containing a pure capacitor: with E=E0 sin(omega*t) across the capacitor, q=CV=CE0 sin(omega*t) (from Kirchhoff's law), and i=dq/dt=omega*C*E0*cos(omega*t)=E0*omega*C*sin(omega*t + pi/2). Comparing with E's equation, current LEADS the EMF by pi/2 (equivalently, E lags i by pi/2) -- the opposite of the inductor case (where voltage leads current)

Phase (phasor) diagram for pure capacitor: E0 and I0 phasors rotate together with angular speed omega, with I0 always pi/2 (90 degrees) ahead of E0. Writing i=I0 sin(omega*t+pi/2) in the same form as Ohm's law (I0=E0/R), the quantity 1/(omega*C) plays the role of resistance, so it is called CAPACITIVE REACTANCE, Xc=1/(omega*C), with SI unit ohm

Capacitive reactance vs. frequency: Xc=1/(omega*C)=1/(2*pi*f*C); higher frequency gives lower Xc. Plotting Xc against f gives Xc*f=1/(2*pi*C)=constant, i.e. a rectangular hyperbola. For DC (f=0), Xc=1/(2*pi*0*C)=infinity -- a capacitor offers infinite resistance to (i.e. completely blocks) DC

Worked numerical (capacitor circuit): a 318 microfarad capacitor is connected to a 230 V, 50 Hz supply. Find capacitive reactance, RMS current, and equations for E and I. Solution: omega=2*pi*50=100*pi rad/s, Xc=1/(omega*C)~10 ohm; Irms=Erms/Xc=230/10=23 A; if E=E0 sin(omega*t), then i=I0 sin(omega*t+pi/2) since current leads voltage, with E0=root(2)*Erms

Average power dissipated in a pure inductor over a complete cycle: instantaneous power P=EI=E0 sin(omega*t)*I0 sin(omega*t - pi/2) (since for an inductor voltage leads current), which simplifies via trig identity to P=-(1/2)E0*I0*sin(2*omega*t). Averaged over a full cycle, the average of sin(2*omega*t) is zero, so average power dissipated in a purely inductive circuit is ZERO over a complete cycle. Even though power dissipation is zero, current still flows -- this current is called WATTLESS CURRENT

Practical use of this zero-power property: to reduce AC current in a circuit while consuming zero (or minimal) power, an inductor is preferred over a resistor -- a resistor would reduce current but dissipate power as heat, whereas an inductor reduces current with (ideally) no power consumption. This is why older tube lights used a choke coil (an inductor) in series rather than a resistor. The same zero-average-power result holds for a pure capacitor as well (instantaneous power P=+(1/2)E0*I0*sin(2*omega*t), again averaging to zero over a complete cycle)

AC circuit containing L and R together (LR circuit): unlike DC, where voltages across series resistors simply add algebraically, VL and VR must be added as VECTORS (phasors), since they are not in phase. Using a phasor diagram: VR is taken along the current direction (in phase with I), VL is drawn 90 degrees ahead (perpendicular) of VR (since voltage across an inductor leads current by pi/2). The resultant (since the angle between VR and VL is 90 degrees) is E=root(VR^2+VL^2)=root((IR)^2+(IXL)^2)=I*root(R^2+XL^2)=IZ, where Z=root(R^2+XL^2) is called the IMPEDANCE of the LR circuit. The phase angle by which E leads I is phi=tan^-1(XL/R), so E=E0 sin(omega*t+phi)

Worked numerical (LR circuit): a coil of inductance L=0.5 H and resistance R=100 ohm is connected to a 240 V, 50 Hz AC supply. Find (a) the maximum current in the coil, and (b) the time lag between the maximum voltage and maximum current. Solution: ZL=root(R^2+(omega*L)^2) with omega=2*pi*50; I0=E0/ZL where E0=240*root(2), giving I0~1.82 A. Phase angle phi=tan^-1(omega*L/R)~57.5 degrees (converted to radians: 57.5*pi/180); time lag=phi/omega~3.19x10^-3 seconds -- meaning the current reaches its maximum this much time AFTER the voltage reaches its maximum

AC circuit containing R and C together (RC circuit): by an analogous phasor derivation to the LR circuit -- VR=IR (in phase with I), VC=I*Xc (but now, since current leads voltage across a capacitor, the phasor diagram has I ahead of VC by 90 degrees, or equivalently VC lags VR by 90 degrees) -- the resultant EMF is epsilon=root(VR^2+VC^2)=I*root(R^2+Xc^2)=I*Zc, where Zc=root(R^2+1/(omega^2*C^2)) is the impedance of the RC circuit. Here current I LEADS the EMF epsilon by phase angle phi (opposite sense from the LR circuit), with tan(phi)=Vc/VR=Xc/R=1/(omega*C*R), so phi=tan^-1(1/(omega*C*R))

Worked numerical (RC circuit, setup and method visible): a circuit connected to a 20 V, 50 Hz supply takes a current of 10 A, with current leading voltage by 1/12 of the time period. Find resistance, capacitive reactance, and capacitance. Method shown: phase angle phi corresponding to a time lead of T/12 is phi=360/12=30 degrees; then R=Zc*cos(phi) (with Zc=E_rms/I_rms from the given 20V, 10A), and similarly Xc follows from Zc and phi, with C then obtained from Xc=1/(omega*C)

markdown_body:
## AC circuit with a pure capacitor (NCERT 7.6)

With $E=E_0\sin(\omega t)$: $q=CE_0\sin(\omega t)$, $i=dq/dt=\omega C E_0\cos(\omega t) = E_0\omega C\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)$.

**Current leads EMF by $\pi/2$** (opposite the inductor case). Writing $i=I_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)$ with $I_0=E_0/X_C$:
$$\boxed{X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C}} \quad\text{(capacitive reactance, unit: ohm)}$$

$X_C f = \dfrac{1}{2\pi C}=$ const $\Rightarrow$ $X_C$ vs. $f$ is a rectangular hyperbola. At $f=0$ (DC), $X_C\to\infty$ — **a capacitor blocks DC**.

**Worked numerical:** $318\,\mu$F, $230$ V, $50$ Hz. $X_C\approx10\,\Omega$; $I_\text{rms}=E_\text{rms}/X_C=230/10=23$ A; $i=I_0\sin(\omega t+\pi/2)$, $E_0=\sqrt2\,E_\text{rms}$.

## Average power in pure L or C: zero (wattless current)

For a pure inductor, $P=EI=E_0I_0\sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega t-\pi/2) = -\tfrac12 E_0I_0\sin(2\omega t)$ — averages to **zero** over a full cycle. Current still flows despite zero power dissipation: this is **wattless current**. (Same result, opposite sign, for a pure capacitor.)

**Practical use:** to reduce AC current with (ideally) no power loss, prefer an inductor over a resistor — old tube lights used a **choke coil** for exactly this reason.

## LR circuit (NCERT 7.7)

$V_R$ and $V_L$ add as **phasors**, not algebraically (they're $90°$ out of phase — $V_L$ leads $V_R$):
$$E = \sqrt{V_R^2+V_L^2} = I\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2} = IZ, \qquad Z=\sqrt{R^2+X_L^2}~\text{(impedance)}$$
$$\phi = \tan^{-1}\frac{X_L}{R}, \qquad E = E_0\sin(\omega t+\phi)$$

**Worked numerical:** coil $L=0.5$ H, $R=100\,\Omega$, on $240$ V, $50$ Hz AC. $Z_L=\sqrt{R^2+(\omega L)^2}$; max current $I_0=E_0/Z_L\approx1.82$ A; phase angle $\phi=\tan^{-1}(\omega L/R)\approx57.5°$; **time lag** $=\phi/\omega\approx3.19\times10^{-3}$ s (current peaks this long after voltage peaks).

## RC circuit (NCERT 7.7)

By analogous phasor reasoning (now $I$ leads $\varepsilon$, since current leads voltage across $C$):
$$\varepsilon = \sqrt{V_R^2+V_C^2} = I\sqrt{R^2+X_C^2} = IZ_C, \qquad Z_C=\sqrt{R^2+\frac{1}{\omega^2C^2}}$$
$$\tan\phi = \frac{X_C}{R}=\frac{1}{\omega CR}, \qquad \phi = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\omega CR}\right)$$

**Worked numerical (setup + method):** circuit on $20$ V, $50$ Hz takes $10$ A, current leading voltage by $T/12$. $\phi = 360°/12=30°$; $R=Z_C\cos\phi$ (with $Z_C=E_\text{rms}/I_\text{rms}$); $X_C$ and hence $C$ follow similarly.

**Second numerical (unfinished in available material):** a $100$ V, $60$ W lamp operated on $220$ V, $50$ Hz mains — find $R$, $X_C$, and $C$ (a lamp-in-series-with-capacitor circuit, used to drop voltage without wasting power in a resistor).
